title: FastAPI: pagination, idempotency, versioning and GraphQL
description: Query-validated pagination, keyset queries in SQLAlchemy, idempotency keys, deprecation headers, router versioning and Strawberry GraphQL with DataLoader.
source: FastAPI documentation (query parameter validation, response headers, APIRouter, deprecated routes); SQLAlchemy 2.0 documentation (tuple_, select); RFC 9745 and RFC 8594; Strawberry documentation (types, DataLoader, FastAPI integration); Stripe idempotency documentation
seriesDescription: Python and FastAPI interview topics in JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short Python/SQL code and multi-correct questions. Python only: nothing here mixes in Java.

questions.prompt: Write a FastAPI GET /items handler named items that takes the query parameters limit (default 20, between 1 and 100) and offset (default 0, at least 0) validated with Query, and returns a dict containing both values.
questions.explanation: Verified with TestClient: limit=500 gives 422 with type less_than_equal. Annotated[int, Query(ge=1, le=100)] is the modern spelling. Capping the page size protects the database from ?limit=1000000.
questions.starter:
from fastapi import FastAPI, Query
app = FastAPI()

questions.prompt: An endpoint takes one-based page numbers and computes the SQLAlchemy clause .limit(25).offset((page - 1) * 25). For page = 4, what OFFSET value is sent to the database?
questions.explanation: (4 - 1) x 25 = 75, so rows 76 to 100 are returned. One-based pages need the - 1; zero-based pages use page x size.

questions.prompt: Models: Post(id, created_at). Write the SQLAlchemy 2.0 statement stmt that selects Post rows strictly older than the cursor pair (last_created_at, last_id) by comparing the tuple (created_at, id), newest first with id as tiebreaker, limited to 21 rows.

checks.label: orders desc by created_at then id

questions.explanation: Verified against SQLite and the SQL it renders: WHERE (created_at, id) < (?, ?). PostgreSQL uses the same row-value syntax with a composite index on (created_at, id). The expanded OR form is equally valid on databases without row values.

questions.prompt: Write a FastAPI POST /payments handler pay(body: PaymentIn, idempotency_key: str = Header(...)). A module-level dict store maps keys to earlier results: if the key was seen return the stored result, otherwise call charge(body), save it under the key, and return it.

checks.label: returns the stored result for a repeated key
saves the new result under the key

questions.explanation: In production the store is Redis or a DB table with a unique constraint on the key, and the check-and-save must be atomic (SET NX or INSERT ... ON CONFLICT), otherwise two concurrent retries both charge. Also store a hash of the body to reject a reused key with a different payload.

questions.prompt: Judge the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: Two retries with the same Idempotency-Key can both reach charge() when they are served by a plain def route that checks a module-level dict and then writes to it.
questions.reason: FastAPI runs plain def routes in a thread pool, and a check followed by a write on a dict is not atomic.

whys.a: Correct: two threads can both pass the "not seen yet" check before either stores its result.
whys.b: Wrong: R is the mechanism behind A.

questions.explanation: Make the claim atomic: a lock around check-and-store for one process, and for several processes a database unique constraint (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING) or Redis SET NX.

questions.prompt: Using FastAPI APIRouter, create routers with the prefixes /v1 and /v2, add a GET /users route to v1 marked deprecated, and mount both routers on app.
questions.starter:
from fastapi import FastAPI, APIRouter
app = FastAPI()
questions.model:
v1 = APIRouter(prefix="/v1")
v2 = APIRouter(prefix="/v2")

@v1.get("/users", deprecated=True)
def users_v1():
    return []

app.include_router(v1)
app.include_router(v2)
questions.explanation: Verified: deprecated=True shows up in the generated OpenAPI. Keep v1 until its Sunset date and log who still calls it before removing it.

questions.prompt: Write a FastAPI GET /v1/users route named users_v1 marked deprecated=True, which takes a response: Response parameter and sets the headers Deprecation and Sunset on it before returning an empty list.
questions.explanation: Verified with TestClient: both headers arrive and the OpenAPI document marks the operation deprecated. RFC 9745 defines the Deprecation date as "@" plus a Unix timestamp; RFC 8594 defines Sunset as an HTTP date.
questions.starter:
from fastapi import FastAPI, Response
app = FastAPI()

questions.prompt: Judge the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: Setting deprecated=True on a FastAPI route marks the operation as deprecated in the generated OpenAPI document.
questions.reason: deprecated=True makes FastAPI answer 410 Gone for that route.

whys.a: Wrong: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.c: Correct: A is true (the docs UI shows it struck through); R is false because the route keeps working normally.

questions.explanation: The flag is documentation only. Pair it with Deprecation and Sunset headers and monitoring of remaining callers.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which changes to a FastAPI v1 API are backward compatible for existing clients?

options.text: Adding a new optional field with a default to a response model.
Renaming the response field fullName to name.
options.why: Clients that read fullName break immediately.

options.text: Adding a new route that v1 clients never call.
Changing id from int to str in a response model.
options.why: Typed clients fail to parse the new type.

options.text: Adding an optional query parameter with a default value.
options.why: Old requests behave exactly as before.

options.text: Making a previously optional request field required.
options.why: Old requests are now rejected with 422.

questions.explanation: Additive changes are safe; renames, type changes, removals and tightened validation are breaking and need a new version or a deprecation period.

questions.prompt: Using Strawberry, define a GraphQL type Book with a title: str field, a Query type with a field books returning list[Book], and build a schema.
questions.explanation: Mount it with strawberry.fastapi.GraphQLRouter(schema) and verify with schema.execute_sync. For N+1 use strawberry.dataloader.DataLoader with a batch load function.

questions.prompt: Write the Strawberry pieces that remove the N+1 on Book.author: an async batch function load_authors(keys: list[int]) that returns authors for all keys with one call authors_by_ids(keys) (assume it returns the list in key order), and a DataLoader named author_loader built from it.
questions.explanation: A resolver then calls await author_loader.load(book.author_id); all load() calls made in the same event-loop tick are batched into one load_authors call. Create the loader per request (for example in the GraphQL context) so its cache does not leak between users.

questions.prompt: A Strawberry DataLoader is created with max_batch_size=10. During one request, a resolver calls loader.load(...) for 25 distinct author ids in the same event-loop tick. How many times is the batch function called?
questions.explanation: Keys are split into batches of at most 10: 10, 10 and 5, so the batch function runs 3 times instead of 25. Verified by running a DataLoader with a recording batch function.

questions.prompt: A GraphQL query asks for books and each book's author. The author resolver throws for one book. What does a typical HTTP GraphQL server return?

options.text: HTTP 200 with partial data and an errors array.
options.why: GraphQL reports field errors in the body; the transport still succeeded.

options.text: HTTP 500 with an empty body, because the resolver crashed the request.
options.why: Field-level exceptions are caught by the engine and reported in errors.
GraphQL has a single endpoint; status codes do not map to fields.

options.text: HTTP 422 with a detail list like FastAPI REST.
options.why: That format belongs to FastAPI request validation, not GraphQL execution.

questions.explanation: Monitoring on status codes alone misses GraphQL failures; inspect the errors array.
